https://www.christiandaily.com/news/roma.text: (Photo: Unsplash) Leaders representing major Christian denominations in Bihor County, Romania, have issued a joint declaration affirming the dignity of every human being while upholding traditional biblical teaching on marriage. Its publication came a day before the Oradea Pride march on Saturday (July 25). The statement, titled "On the Dignity of the Human Person," was signed by Orthodox, Roman Catholic, Greek Catholic, Reformed, Pentecostal, and Baptist leaders in the region. It sought to outline a unified Christian perspective on human identity and sexuality amid ongoing public debates in western Romania. "In the context of public debates and demonstrations touching upon some of the most sensitive dimensions of human existence, we, representatives of the religious denominations in Bihor County, feel it is our duty to express our vision - not to impose it nor to condemn individuals, but out of a responsibility to testify, with respect and love, to the truth about humanity," the statement reads. The leaders unequivocally affirmed the intrinsic value of all individuals, stating that every person is created in the image of God and therefore "possesses a dignity that can neither be negotiated nor lost.” "No one has the right to hate, despise, or turn a fellow human being into an adversary," the declaration said, noting that judgement belongs strictly to God. Addressing the theological foundation of human identity, the statement rejected reducing a person's existence solely to sexuality or passing desires. "Christian teaching has always affirmed that the practice of homosexual relations is incompatible with the order of creation, like any other use of sexuality outside the communion between a man and a woman united through Holy Matrimony," the leaders wrote, adding that this doctrine stems not from hostility, but from the conviction that God knows the true purpose of human existence. The statement also contained an acknowledgment of past shortcomings within the Church, calling ministers to humility. "We acknowledge that, not infrequently, we failed to welcome such wounds with the delicacy of the Gospel," the text reads. "There were moments when sterile rigors took precedence over parental embraces, and harsh responses came faster than benevolent listening." Calling on believers to respond to cultural shifts "without hatred, without verbal violence, without irony, and without contempt," the declaration urged Christians to bear witness with gentleness, warning that "truth without love becomes cruelty, and love without truth turns into a simple endorsement of error." The declaration was signed by P.S. Sofronie (Romanian Orthodox Bishop of Oradea), P.S. László Böcskei (Roman Catholic Bishop of Oradea), P.S. Virgil Bercea (Greek-Catholic Bishop of Oradea), P.S. Bogdán Szabolcs János (Reformed Bishop), Pastor Ioan Moldovan (President of the Pentecostal Community of Oradea), and Pastor Mihai Micula (President of the Baptist Community of Oradea). https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/HL2608/S.text: Scoop Werewolf Wellington The Dig Business Scoop Pacific Community Review of Books InfoPages Front Page Scoops Parliament Politics Regional Business Sci-Tech World Culture Education Health Front Page Scoops Parliament Politics Regional Business Sci-Tech World Culture Education Health Scoop Werewolf Wellington Scoop The Dig Business Scoop Pacific Community Review of Books InfoPages Book Reviews | Gordon Campbell | Scoop News | Wellington Scoop | Community Scoop | Search Exonerating Murder: The IDF And The World Central Kitchen Killings Being a resident in Gaza has proved lethal not merely for civilians eking out a wretched existence. Mortality rates among journalists, medical staff, and aid workers have been egregiously high since Israel’s military opened its account after the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023. (In truth, Israel’s account regarding striking, bombing and embargoing this little strip of territory has been open for decades.) The regularity of killings, largely at the hands of the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF), negatives the claim that there isn’t a policy or approach in place that forgoes the rigours of international humanitarian law in favour of murderous resolution. The IDF, and its foam flecked supporters, always insist that international law is something observed, though no one quite seems to know what version is being applied. The killing of seven staff working for World Central Kitchen on April 1, 2024 illustrates the matter in grimmest fashion. Members of the charity – three Britons, a dual US-Canadian national, a Pole, an Australian and a Palestinian – had unloaded humanitarian food supplies from Cyprus intended for residents in Gaza. Their convoy, with the WCK logo prominently displayed on the vehicles, was travelling in a designated “deconflicted” zone when it was attacked by three missiles fired from a Hermes 450 drone. The charity had also been coordinating their movements with the IDF with their usual diligence. Advertisement - scroll to continue reading On August 19, the IDF announced that the case had been closed after finding “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify opening a criminal investigation or the taking of additional measures against any of those involved in the incident”. The spokesperson’s remarks were instructive, lauding the role of the spurious General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism (FFAM), with its keenness on conducting “factual assessments of exceptional operational incidents, while using a range of tools and methodologies.” Some 150 incidents had been reviewed by the FFAM since the war began, and those behind the WCK deaths were to be spared legal scrutiny. Indeed, the IDF was not above libelling the workers, suggesting that it had “identified a gunman on a truck in the humanitarian aid convoy while it was on route to a warehouse for the unloading of the aid.” In a worrying reflection on the alleged expertise of the IDF, the troops in question had also “identified vehicles surrounding the trucks in a manner that, in their assessment, and based on accumulated operational experience, corresponded to a scenario in which the Hamas terrorist organization had taken control of the convoy.” While there had been “serious failures in the process that led to the assessment that Hamas operatives were travelling in the vehicles” (grotesque understatement) the decisions made by the commanders raised no “reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct”; there were sufficient, extenuating “suspicious indicators”. The only seedy conclusion to reach here is that misidentifying humanitarians, misapplying alleged experiences gathered in battle, and committing calculated murder are habits in the field. Blatant errors – if they can be called that – are pardonable. The object here: categorise and exterminate. The refusal by the military prosecutors to institute criminal proceedings provoked an unusually salty note of anger from Australia’s Foreign Minister Penny Wong. Australia had been “outraged” at the decision, noting the fate of one of its nationals, Zomi Frankcom. The refusal to pursue matters had been made despite the admission by the IDF that its “strikes on Zomi and her colleagues’ vehicles were the result of serious failures to follow IDF procedures, mistaken identification and errors in decision making.” The timing of the announcement – made on World Humanitarian Day – was exquisite, suggesting either a concerted callousness on the part of the Israeli authorities, or dollops of black humour. Wong was not impressed. “The Australian Government learned of Israel’s decision late last night, moments before it was announced, on World Humanitarian Day – which is especially insulting to Zomi’s loved ones, humanitarians and all Australians.” A joint statement by the foreign ministries of Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom released on August 21 also denounced the decision not to consider the case further as “shameful”. Gone from it were the guarded qualifications that had been expressed in 2024. “The World Central Kitchen attack is one of countless incidents in Gaza where there has been no accountability.” In 2025, despite a ceasefire, 186 humanitarian workers had been killed. The Polish foreign ministry, reflecting on the death of one of their nationals, Damian Soból, also expressed its dismay. “Partnership requires respect,” stated foreign minister Radosław Sikorski with unmistakable bluntness. “The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, as well as the failure of accountability for IDF’s excessive use of force are undermining public support in even pro-Israel nations.” In its pungent statement on the affair, World Central Kitchen expressed its fundamental disagreement with the decision, regarding it as “inconsistent with the truth and deeply offensive.” The IDF had known that the organisation’s workers were “unarmed and posing a threat to nobody. It had full visual clarity on our clearly marked humanitarian vehicles during the extended, multiple airstrikes. It knew our team’s movements, identities and activities in advance.” The military investigation had been shoddy, conflating “different timelines and events” while muddying the narrative. “We continue,” the statement goes on to say, “to demand an independent commission to investigate the airstrikes because the IDF cannot credibly investigate its own conduct.” The Military Police have decided, instead, to focus on two other cases: the killing of 6-year-old Hind Rajab along with six of her family members and two medics in Gaza City in January 2024; and the slaying of 15 rescue workers as part of a convoy of emergency vehicles and ambulances in Rafah in March last year. Best not hold out too much hope for a just resolution of those cases. Dr. Binoy Kampmark was a Commonwealth Scholar at Selwyn College, Cambridge. He currently lectures at RMIT University. Photograph: US Air Force/PA US military US fighter jet crashes at air base in western Germany Officials say one pilot safely ejected as F-16 believed to have crashed on approach to Spangdahlem after training drill Reuters Tue 22 Sep 2026 12.49 EDT Last modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 16.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google ⁠An F-16 fighter jet assigned to the US air ⁠base Spangdahlem ⁠in ​western Germany crashed on Tuesday, the US military said, ⁠adding that one pilot had ejected safely and was receiving ⁠medical treatment. The cause of the incident ​is under ‌investigation, the military ‌said in a statement, with ‌emergency response personnel at the scene of the crash. Germany’s air traffic control authority, in a separate statement, said a total of four F-16s ‌had been taking part in a training exercise. “Two were still ​in the training area, while two were returning to Spangdahlem air base. One of these two jets ⁠is believed to have crashed while ​on ​approach,” it said, ​adding the remaining F-16s had landed ​at ‌the US aAir ​Force base in Ramstein.
